# Rectangular matrix multiplication from polynomial products

**Abstract**

In this note, we extend the matrix-multiplication analysis in [9] to rectangular products and prove

In particular, \(\omega(1,\frac{1}{2},1)=2\) and the dual exponent satisfies \(\alpha\ge\frac{1}{2}\). The proof uses explicit degenerations of convolution tensors, multinomial counting, and Strassen’s spectral theorem. An angular constraint on three dot-product parameters gives both the rectangular curve and a bound for \(\omega(a,b,c)\), with exact exponent _a+b_ whenever \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\) and \(c\le\frac{ab}{a+b}\). As an application, Zwick’s algorithm [15] for all-pairs shortest paths in directed unweighted graphs runs in _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time. Combining the rectangular bound with the (min,+)-product improvement of Alman and Vassilevska Williams [1] further gives _O(n_<sup>2.4999</sup>) running time.

### 1. Introduction

Disclaimer. This note, its proofs, analysis and writeup were obtained fully through OpenAI x (GPT-6.1). The author has read and analyzed this note in full and takes full responsibility for its contents, and takes no credit for this work.

The initial motivation for this note was to explore whether the methods of the ground- breaking matrix-multiplication result in [9] could be pushed to analyze rectangular matrix products. We also aim to gather useful bounds and their algorithmic consequences in one place. Rephrasing the proofs in a form accessible to the theoretical computer science community has value in its own right.

### Complexity convention.

Throughout this note, all complexity bounds suppress a +_o_(1) term in the exponent: _O(nc_) denotes _nc+o_(1). All shape parameters are fixed.

Rectangular matrix multiplication is a basic ingredient in algorithms for all-pairs problems, including shortest paths, lowest common ancestors, and Hamming distance. Its exponents depend on the shape of the product; an improvement for square matrices need not give a comparable improvement for every rectangular shape. The analysis in [9] establishes the square bound \(\omega\le 2.25\) using a shared-leg entropy inequality and degenerations of convolution tensors. We extend that analysis to rectangular products by retaining the orientation information lost under full leg symmetrization.

We work over C. The resulting exponent bounds hold over every field of characteristic zero by invariance of asymptotic tensor rank under field extension [10, Theorem 3.10].

For fixed nonnegative real _u,v,w_, let \(\omega(u,v,w)\) be the infimum of the exponents _e_ for which multiplying an \(\lceil n^u\rceil\times\lceil n^v\rceil\) matrix by a \(\lceil n^v\rceil\times\lceil n^w\rceil\) matrix uses _O(n<sup>e</sup>_) arithmetic operations, with the convention above. Write \(\omega(k)=\omega(1,k,1)\) and \(\alpha=sup\{k\ge 0:\omega(k)=2\}\).

We first state the bound for general matrix shapes, with the exponents sorted in decreasing order. We interpret the threshold \(\frac{ab}{a+b}\) as zero when _a=b_=0.

**Theorem 1.1.** _For every fixed_ \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\),

\(\omega(a,b,c)\le\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
a+b, & c\le\frac{ab}{a+b}, \\
\frac{a+b+c}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{ab}{c}+\frac{ac}{b}+\frac{bc}{a}\right), & c>\frac{ab}{a+b}.
\end{array}\right.\) (1)

_When_ \(c\le\frac{ab}{a+b}\)_, equality holds by the size lower bound._

Applying this bound to the sorted dimensions of (1_,k,_1) gives the rectangular curve.

**Corollary 1.2.** _For every fixed real_ \(k\ge 0\),

\(\omega(k)\le\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
2, & 0\le k\le\frac{1}{2}, \\
1+k+\frac{1}{4k}, & k\ge\frac{1}{2}.
\end{array}\right.\) (2)

_Consequently_ \(\omega(k)=2\) _for_ \(0\le k\le\frac{1}{2}\).

Corollary 1.2 gives exponent two for inner dimension up to _n_<sup>0.5</sup>, and an upper bound within \(\frac{1}{4k}\) of the input-size lower bound 1+_k_ for \(k\ge 1\).

The proof has two parts. First, we list explicit ways to split and combine polynomial products and apply a tensor character to them. A character assigns numerical sizes that add on direct sums, multiply on tensor products, and cannot increase under restriction. Multinomial counting gives concavity and growth inequalities for these sizes. Rescaling, common slopes, and affine bounds then give \(\sum_iarccos\sqrt{p_i}\ge\pi/2\) for the character’s three dot-product parameters.

Second, Wolstenholme’s inequality bounds weighted sums of these parameters. We apply Strassen’s spectral theorem: the largest character value equals asymptotic tensor rank. We state precisely the form of this theorem we use, then show how the rank bound gives a running-time bound for every fixed matrix shape.

#### Relation to the preceding analysis.

The two polynomial splittings in Lemma 2.1 recap the proofs of Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 of \[9\] in coefficient coordinates. The finite separation adapts Proposition 3.1 of that reference. All three constructions are proved in the appendices. Multinomial counting then gives the required power-sum inequality. The replication construction, rescaling, and coupling of six affine offsets supply the rectangular extension. The weighted bound uses the classical Wolstenholme inequality \[8\]. Strassen’s spectral theorem is a standard input; a modern exposition is \[12\]. We cite it rather than reproduce its proof. We make no priority claim for the standard tools or the finite construction variants. Section 7 substitutes the bounds into known algorithmic tradeoffs.

## 2. Polynomial products and finite constructions

We begin by describing matrix multiplication and convolution as tensors. We then build ways to split polynomial products and separate computations that share variables. These constructions give the inequalities in Section 3. A further construction replicates a convolution; it will let us compare convolutions at different scales in Section 4.

A tensor is a trilinear form in three groups of variables, called its _legs_. A _restriction_ makes linear substitutions independently on the three legs. A _degeneration_ is a limit of such restrictions: the substitutions may depend on \(\varepsilon\neq 0\), and every resulting coefficient converges as \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\). Our constructions first change bases and then multiply variables by integer powers of \(\varepsilon\). The resulting coefficient array is a polynomial in \(\varepsilon\) whose constant coefficient is the desired tensor. We write \(T\ge S\) for a restriction and \(T\unknown S\) for a degeneration. Successive constructions can use a single parameter: replace the earlier parameter by a sufficiently large power of the later one, so every earlier error term still has positive total exponent.

The rank(_T_) is the least number of products of three linear forms, one per leg, summing to _T_. The direct sum \(S\oplus T\) uses disjoint variables on all three legs and represents independent computations. The tensor product \(S\otimes T\) pairs their indices, as in a Kronecker product, and represents their composition on blocks. We write _mT_ for _m_ independent copies, and \(T^{\otimes N}\) for _N_ tensor factors. Thus \(\text{rank}(T)xyz\ge T\). All factors used below restrict to _xyz_ by keeping one nonzero term; this is what it means to drop a factor.

The oriented dot products are<tbc>

\(B_X(q)=x\sum_{j=1}^qy_jz_j,\)

<tbc>with _B<sub>Y</sub>(q),B<sub>Z</sub>(q_) obtained by permuting the legs. They have rank _q_, and \(B_i(q)\otimes B_i(q')\) is \(B_i(qq')\) after reindexing. The matrix multiplication tensor factors as

\(\langle A,B,C\rangle=\sum_{u,v,w}x_{uv}y_{vw}z_{wu}\cong B_Y(A)\otimes B_Z(B)\otimes B_X(C).\) (3)

Thus the three dot-product dimensions specify the matrix shape.

For distinct input legs _i,j_, with remaining output leg _k_, the _convolution tensor_ is<tbc>

\(C_{ij}(r,s)=\sum_{h=0}^{r-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{s-1}x_h^{(i)}x_\ell^{(j)}x_{h+\ell}^{(k)}.\)

It multiplies two polynomials represented by their coefficient vectors. Its rank is _r+s_-1: evaluation at _r+s_-1 points and interpolation give the upper bound, and the independent output coefficients give the matching matrix-rank lower bound. Decreasing either input length is a restriction. Also

\(C_{ij}(1,s)\cong B_i(s),C_{ij}(r,1)\cong B_j(r).\) (4)

Blocks _T<sub>h</sub>_ are _matched sectors sharing leg i_ when \(T=\sum_hT_h\) and the blocks may share variables on leg _i_, but use pairwise disjoint variables on each other leg. The following constructions hold for every permutation of the legs.

**Lemma 2.1** (Finite separation and polynomial splittings)**.**

1. _If T has M matched sectors sharing leg i, then_<tbc>

\((2M)T\unknown\oplus_{h=1}^M(T_h\otimes B_i(M)).\) \(\text{(5)}\)

_The sectors on the right are independent on all three legs._<tbc>

_2._ _For_ \(r\ge 1\) _and_ \(s\ge 2\), \(C_{ij}(r,s)\otimes B_i(2)\) _degenerates to two matched sectors sharing leg i, namely C<sub>ij</sub>(r,s_+1) _and C<sub>ij</sub>(r,s_-1).<tbc>

_3._ _For_ \(r,s\ge 1\), _C<sub>ij</sub>(r,_3_s+r_-1) _degenerates to three matched sectors sharing leg i: two copies of C<sub>ij</sub>(r,s_) _and one copy of C<sub>ik</sub>(r,s)._

Appendices A and B give the polynomial splittings in coefficient coordinates. Appendix C proves (5) using a finite geometric sum and a nonnegative square. The next construction splits a convolution into repeated independent copies of a smaller convolution.

**Lemma 2.2** (Replicating a convolution)**.** _For all positive integers m,r,s,_

\(C_{ij}(mr,ms)\unknown mC_{ij}(r,s).\) (6)

The construction combines polynomial division with the standard evaluation description of cyclic convolution \[5, Theorem 5 and Section 5.1\]. We give the full proof in Appendix E.

## 3. Tensor characters and counting

To use the preceding constructions, we assign numerical values to tensors using tensor characters. The splittings and separation give concavity and tripling inequalities for their convolution values, which we rescale in the next section. We also identify the three parameters that determine their matrix-multiplication values and state Strassen’s theorem: bounding every character value will give an asymptotic rank bound in Section 6.

A _tensor character_ is a function \(\lambda\) from tensors to nonnegative real numbers satisfying

\(\begin{array}{ c c c }
\lambda(S\oplus T) & = & \lambda(S)+\lambda(T), \\
 &  & S\ge T \Longrightarrow & \lambda(S)\ge\lambda(T).
\end{array}\) (7)

These rules express addition of independent computations, multiplication of tensor factors, and monotonicity under linear substitutions. Matrix rank after grouping one leg against the other two is an example. Keeping one nonzero term and using \(\text{rank}(T)xyz\ge T\) gives \(1\le\lambda(T)\le\text{rank}(T)\) for every nonzero _T_.

**Lemma 3.1** (Interpolation of a degeneration)**.** _Suppose a degeneration_ \(T\vartriangleleft S\) _produces a tensor_ \(P(\varepsilon)\) _whose coefficients are polynomials of degree at most L. Then, for every integer_ \(N\ge 1\),

\((NL+1)T^{\otimes N}\ge S^{\otimes N}.\) (8)

_Consequently, every tensor character satisfies_ \(\lambda(S)\le\lambda(T)\).

Equation (8) is the standard interpolation conversion from degeneration to restriction \[2, Theorem 8\], applied to tensor powers. We include the proof for completeness in Appendix D.

The _asymptotic rank_ of _T_ is

\(\widetilde{R}(T)=lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} rank(T^{\otimes N})^{1/N}=inf_{N\ge 1}rank(T^{\otimes N})^{1/N}.\)

The limit exists because tensor rank is submultiplicative; apply the subadditive-sequence form of Fekete’s lemma to its logarithm.

**Theorem 3.2** (Strassen’s spectral theorem)**.** _For every nonzero tensor T over_ C,

\(\widetilde{R}(T)=max_\lambda\lambda(T),\) (9)

_where the maximum ranges over all tensor characters._

We use \[10, Theorem 3.8\]; see also \[12, Corollary 3.30 of the author version\]. The easy direction follows from \(\lambda(T)^N=\lambda(T^{\otimes N})\le rank(T^{\otimes N})\). The theorem supplies the opposite direction. Thus, to prove an upper bound on asymptotic rank, it suffices to bound every character value.

Fix an arbitrary character \(\lambda\). Its _dot-product parameters_ are \(p_i=log_2\lambda(B_i(2))\in[0,1]\), for _i=X,Y,Z_. They determine the values at all integer dimensions:<tbc>

\(\lambda(B_i(q))=q^{p_i}(q\ge 1).\) (10)

<tbc>The interval \[0,1\] follows from \(1\le\lambda(B_i(2))\le 2\). Tensor powers turn multiplication of dimensions into multiplication of character values; comparison with powers of two then gives (10). Appendix F gives the details. In particular, (3) gives<tbc>

\(\lambda(\langle A,B,C\rangle)=A^{p_Y}B^{p_Z}C^{p_X}.\) (11)

<tbc>Our aim is to constrain these three parameters for every character. Define its _convolution profiles_ by

\(f_{ij}(r,s)=\lambda(C_{ij}(r,s)).\) (12)

The next counting argument turns the polynomial splittings into inequalities for these profiles.

Suppose _T_ splits into _s_ matched sectors _T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>s</sub>_ sharing leg _i_. In \(T^{\otimes N}\) a sector is specified by a word of _N_ sector labels. Retain on the two nonshared legs the words with _n<sub>h</sub>_ occurrences of label _h_, where \(\sum_hn_h=N\). There are<tbc>

\(M=\left(\begin{array}{ c }
N \\
n_1,\dots,n_s
\end{array}\right)\)

<tbc>matched sectors. For example, multiplicities (2,1) give the words 112,121,211. Each sector is a product of the _T<sub>h</sub>_ with the prescribed multiplicities. Apply (5); now all legs distinguish the words, so their factors can be reordered independently. This gives

\((2M)T^{\otimes N}\vartriangleleft M\left(\otimes_hT_h^{\otimes n_h}\right)\otimes B_i(M).\) (13)

**Lemma 3.3** (Multinomial power-sum inequality)**.** _If_ \(T\unknown\sum_{h=1}^sT_h\) _is a splitting into matched sectors sharing leg i and p<sub>i</sub>\>_0_, then_

\(\lambda(T)^{1/p_i}\ge\sum_h\lambda(T_h)^{1/p_i}.\) (14)

_For fully independent summands,_ \(T\unknown\oplus_hT_h\) _gives_ \(\lambda(T)\ge\sum_h\lambda(T_h)\) _directly by additivity._

The counting idea is to sum over all multiplicities. With \(a_h=\lambda(T_h)^{1/p_i}\), applying the character to (13) and using the multinomial theorem gives

\(\left(\sum_ha_h\right)^N\le(N+1)^s2^{1/p_i}\lambda(T)^{N/p_i}.\)

The number of multiplicity tuples is polynomial in _N_, so it disappears when we take _N_-th roots and let \(N\rightarrow\infty\). The full calculation is in Appendix F.

Rank bounds and restrictions give

\(1\le f_{ij}(r,s)\le r+s-1,f_{ij}(r,s)=f_{ji}(s,r),\) (15)

and coordinatewise monotonicity. The equality merely interchanges the two polynomial inputs of the same convolution.

**Lemma 3.4** (Powered concavity and tripling)**.** _For p<sub>i</sub>\>_0_, the sequence_ \(s\mapsto f_{ij}(r,s)^{1/p_i}\) _is concave, and for all integers_ \(r,s\ge 1\),

\(f_{ij}(r,3s+r-1)^{1/p_i}\ge 2f_{ij}(r,s)^{1/p_i}+f_{ik}(r,s)^{1/p_i},\) (16)

_where i,j,k are distinct. For p<sub>j</sub>\>_0_, the sequence_ \(r\mapsto f_{ij}(r,s)^{1/p_j}\) _is also concave._

For example, the two-sector splitting gives

\(2f_{ij}(r,s)^{1/p_i}\ge f_{ij}(r,s+1)^{1/p_i}+f_{ij}(r,s-1)^{1/p_i},\)

which is discrete concavity. The three-sector splitting gives (16); input interchange gives concavity in the other coordinate. Appendix F supplies the proof.

## 4. Rescaling the convolution profiles

We next pass from integer input lengths to real ones, so we can compare convolution shapes at any scale. Replication from Section 2 lets us enlarge both inputs together; the bounds, monotonicity, concavity, and tripling inequalities from the preceding section control the resulting limit. We obtain continuous profiles that retain concavity and tripling and scale linearly when both lengths grow by the same factor.

Applying a character to Lemma 2.2 gives

\(f_{ij}(mr,ms)\ge mf_{ij}(r,s).\) (17)

This makes the rescaled values stable under further replication. For real _r,s\>_0, define

\(g_{ij}(r,s)=lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\frac{f_{ij}(\lceil mr\rceil,\lceil ms\rceil)}{m},m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.\) (18)

The following lemma justifies this limit and lets us work with real lengths throughout the remaining analysis.

**Lemma 4.1** (Rescaled profiles)**.** _The limit in_ (18) _exists. The profiles g<sub>ij</sub> are continuous, coordinatewise nondecreasing, and satisfy_<tbc>

\(min\{r,s\}\le g_{ij}(r,s)\le r+s,g_{ij}(r,s)=g_{ji}(s,r),g_{ij}(tr,ts)=tg_{ij}(r,s).\) (19)

<tbc>_For p<sub>i</sub>\>_0, \(g_{ij}^{1/p_i}\) _is concave in s and satisfies_

\(g_{ij}(r,3s+r)^{1/p_i}\ge 2g_{ij}(r,s)^{1/p_i}+g_{ik}(r,s)^{1/p_i}.\) (20)

_For p<sub>j</sub>\>_0, \(g_{ij}^{1/p_j}\) _is concave in r. All lengths and scale factors here may be arbitrary positive reals._

The discrete inequalities thus become inequalities about homogeneous curves. The additive -1 in (16) disappears at this scale. The proof first compares rational lengths at a common integer scale; homogeneity and monotonicity then give continuity and the real extension. Appendix F includes that argument and verifies that rounding the lengths in (18) does not change the limit.

## 5. Common slopes and the angular constraint

With the profile properties from Lemma 4.1, we can now relate the three dot-product parameters \(p_i\in[0,1]\). Comparing the growth of differently oriented convolutions leads to the angular constraint in Proposition 5.2. This is the only result from this section needed for the running-time bounds in Section 6.

Index the three tensor legs by 1,2,3. Full proofs of this section’s slope and growth claims are in Appendix G.

**Lemma 5.1** (Common slopes and affine bounds)**.** _Fix i with p<sub>i</sub>\>_0_, and let j,k be the other legs. The functions P<sub>ij</sub>(s_)=_g<sub>ij</sub>_(1_,s_)<sup>1_/p<sub>i</sub>_</sup> _and P<sub>ik</sub>(s_)=_g<sub>ik</sub>_(1_,s_)<sup>1_/p<sub>i</sub>_</sup> _have a common asymptotic slope L<sub>i</sub>\>_0_. There are offsets satisfying_<tbc>

\(c_{ij},c_{ik}\ge 0,c_{ij}+c_{ik}\le 1,\) (21)

<tbc>_such that, for all real s,t\>_0,

\(P_{ij}(s+t)\ge P_{ij}(s)+L_it,L_is\le P_{ij}(s)\le L_i(s+c_{ij}),\)

_and likewise for P<sub>ik</sub>._

Concavity gives each curve a limiting slope. The coupled tripling inequalities force the two slopes to agree. Writing _R=P<sub>ij</sub>+P<sub>ik</sub>_, they also give \(R(3s+1)\ge 3R(s)\); iteration yields \(R(s)\le L_i(2s+1)\). Consequently the two curves stay above their common limiting line, and their normalized vertical offsets are nondecreasing with sum at most one. Their limits are _c<sub>ij</sub>,c<sub>ik</sub>_. This explains both the affine bounds and the constraint on their sum.

**Proposition 5.2** (Angular constraint)**.** _The dot-product parameters of every tensor character satisfy_

\(\sum_{i=1}^3arccos\sqrt{p_i}\ge\frac{\pi}{2}.\) (22)

_Proof outline._ If some _p<sub>i</sub>_=0, its summand is already \(\pi/2\). Assume all three parameters are positive. For this outline, suppose _g=g<sub>ij</sub>_ is differentiable. The increment and upper bounds in<tbc>

Lemma 5.1 give \(P'_{ij}(t)\ge L_i\) and \(P_{ij}(t)\le L_i(t+c_{ij})\). Homogeneity gives _g(r,s_)=_rPij(s/r)pi_, so, also interchanging the inputs, \(\frac{\partial_sg(r,s)}{g(r,s)}=\frac{p_i}{r}\frac{P'_{ij}(s/r)}{P_{ij}(s/r)}\ge\frac{p_i}{s+c_{ij}r},\)
\(\frac{\partial_rg(r,s)}{g(r,s)}=\frac{p_j}{s}\frac{P'_{ji}(r/s)}{P_{ji}(r/s)}\ge\frac{p_j}{r+c_{ji}s}.\) Differentiating _g(tr,ts_)=_tg(r,s_) at _t_=1 gives \(r\frac{\partial_rg(r,s)}{g(r,s)}+s\frac{\partial_sg(r,s)}{g(r,s)}=1.\) Substituting the two lower bounds yields \(1\ge\frac{p_is}{s+c_{ij}r}+\frac{p_jr}{r+c_{ji}s}(r,s>0).\) (23) Appendix G obtains the same inequality using finite increments, without assuming differentiability. Clearing denominators gives a quadratic in _r/s_. Its nonnegativity for every positive ratio implies \(\sqrt{c_{ij}c_{ji}}\ge\left(\sqrt{p_ip_j}-\sqrt{(1-p_i)(1-p_j)}\right)_+,\) (24) where (_z_)+=max{_z,_0}. For nonnegative _x_1_,x_2_,x_3, AM-GM and (21) give \(\sum_{i0\). Then (24) gives \(\sqrt{c_{ij}c_{ji}}\ge cos(\theta_i+\theta_j)\). Using the product-to-sum identities, we get \(cos(\theta_i+\theta_j)x_j+cos(\theta_i+\theta_k)x_k=cos\theta_i+\frac{cos(\theta_i+2\theta_j)+cos(\theta_i+2\theta_k)}{2}\)
\(=x_i+cosScos(\theta_j-\theta_k)>x_i.\) The extra term is positive: cos_S\>_0 and \(cos(\theta_j-\theta_k)>0\), since \(|\theta_j-\theta_k|\le S<\pi/2\). Multiplying by _xi_ and summing contradicts (25). Appendix G contains the complete proof, including the quadratic calculation. ## 6. From character bounds to running times We can now turn the parameter constraint into matrix-multiplication algorithms. The other ingredients are the matrix-tensor formula (11) and Strassen’s spectral theorem (Theorem 3.2). For a given matrix shape, we bound a weighted sum of the three parameters for every character; the theorem then bounds asymptotic rank. We first show how this rank bound gives a running-time bound, then apply the angular constraint from Proposition 5.2 to obtain the general-shape bound and the rectangular curve. **Lemma 6.1** (Character bounds give algorithms)**.** _Fix_ \(\mathbf{h}=(h_X,h_Y,h_Z)\ge 0\)_. If the dot- product parameters of every tensor character satisfy_ \(\sum_ih_ip_i\le E\)_, then_ \(\omega(h_Y,h_Z,h_X)\le E\).

_Proof._ The zero target is trivial. For a fixed integer \(N\ge 2\), put \(D_i=\lceil N^{h_i}\rceil\) and \(M_N=\otimes_iB_i(D_i)\). Since \(D_i\le 2N^{h_i}\) and \(0\le p_i\le 1\), every character satisfies<tbc>

\(\lambda(M_N)=\prod_iD_i^{p_i}\le 8N\sum_ih_ip_i\le 8N^E.\)

<tbc>Theorem 3.2 therefore gives

\(\widetilde{R}(M_N)\le 8N^E.\) (26)

Fix any positive exponent slack \(\eta\). First choose _N_ so large that \(8<N^{\eta/2}\). The infimum defining \(\widetilde{R}(M_N)\) then gives a fixed integer _K_ and an exact rank decomposition with

\(R:=rank(M_N^{\otimes K})\le N^{K(E+\eta)}.\)

This is a finite bilinear algorithm for matrix dimensions \((D_Y^K,D_Z^K,D_X^K)\). Apply it recursively \(\ell\) times to blocks. By (3), the resulting dimensions are \((D_Y^{K\ell},D_Z^{K\ell},D_X^{K\ell})\) and there are \(R^\ell\) scalar multiplications.

Each input and output dimension, viewed as a number of scalar entries, is at most _R_, by the corresponding matrix-rank lower bound. Thus the linear substitutions and additions over all recursion levels use \(O(\ell R^\ell)\) operations. Given input size _n_, choose \(\ell=\lceil log_Nn/K\rceil\) and pad to these dimensions. They cover the target shape because \(D_i^{K\ell}\ge n^{h_i}\), while \(R^\ell=O(n^{E+\eta})\). This proves the bound for every positive slack, and hence the lemma under our exponent convention. All choices of _N_, _K_, and the finite identity precede the limit \(n\rightarrow\infty\).

It remains to bound these weighted sums using the angular constraint.

_Proof of Theorem 1.1._ Reorder the character’s dot-product parameters so that the objective is _ap_<sub>1</sub>+_bp_<sub>2</sub>+_cp_<sub>3</sub>, and write \(p_i=cos^2\theta_i\) with \(\theta_i\in[0,\pi/2]\). By Proposition 5.2, their sum is at least \(\pi/2\). Decreasing angles to make the sum exactly \(\pi/2\) only increases the objective, so it suffices to bound that case. If _b_=0, then _c_=0 and the objective is at most _a_.

For _a,b,c\>_0, put \(\beta_i=2\theta_i\) and<tbc>

\(u=\sqrt{\frac{bc}{a}},v=\sqrt{\frac{ac}{b}},w=\sqrt{\frac{ab}{c}}.\)

<tbc>Thus _vw=a_, _wu=b_, _uv=c_, and \(\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3=\pi\). Wolstenholme’s inequality \[8, Equation (1)\], applied with weights _u,v,w_, gives<tbc>

\(2(acos\beta_1+bcos\beta_2+ccos\beta_3)\le u^2+v^2+w^2.\)

<tbc>The inequality also holds at zero angles by continuity. Since \(p_i=(1+cos\beta_i)/2\), it gives

\(ap_1+bp_2+cp_3\le\frac{a+b+c}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{ab}{c}+\frac{ac}{b}+\frac{bc}{a}\right).\)

For _a,b\>_0, set \(c_0=\frac{ab}{a+b}\). If \(0\le c\le c_0\), replace _c_ in the objective by _c_<sub>0</sub>, which only increases it. The displayed bound at _c_<sub>0</sub> equals _a+b_. This proves both branches, including _c_=0.

We have bounded the objective for every tensor character. Lemma 6.1, with target **h**=(_c,a,b_), gives (1).

_Proof of Corollary 1.2._ Apply Theorem 1.1 to the sorted dimensions of (1_,k,_1). For \(0\le k\le 1\), the first branch applies exactly when \(k\le\frac{1}{2}\). In the remaining range, both possible orderings give

\(\frac{2+k}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\left(2k+\frac{1}{k}\right)=1+k+\frac{1}{4k}.\)

The output-size lower bound \(\omega(k)\ge 2\) proves equality for \(0\le k\le\frac{1}{2}\) and hence \(\alpha\ge\frac{1}{2}\).

Some values of the bound in Corollary 1.2 are:

The exponent convention gives an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>)-time algorithm at \(k=\frac{1}{2}\).

## 7. Applications

Corollary 1.2 and Theorem 1.1 give the following bounds through standard rectangular- multiplication balances. All bounds use arithmetic operations, with graph operations and symbol comparisons also charged.

1. **One lowest common ancestor per pair in a DAG.** Grandoni et al. \[4, Theorem 4.2 of the published version\] obtain exponent 1+2_x_ from the balance \(\omega(x)=3x\). Corol lary 1.2 permits \(x=(1+\sqrt{3})/4\), giving \(O(n^{(3+\sqrt{3})/2})\) time for finding one lowest common ancestor for every pair in an _n_-vertex DAG. The exponent is \((3+\sqrt{3})/2\approx 2.36603\).<tbc>

2. **Exact all-pairs Hamming distance.** For _n_ vectors of length _n_ over an unrestricted alphabet, the reduction to dominance products \[7\] and Yuster’s tradeoff \[13, Proposition 2.1\] give the balance \(\rho=\omega(4-\rho)\). Corollary 1.2 gives \(\rho=(13-\sqrt{7})/4\approx 2.58856\) and running time \(O(n^\rho)\) for computing every exact Hamming distance.<tbc>

3. **The standard unweighted APSP balance.** Zwick’s deterministic algorithm for directed unweighted APSP \[15, Section 6\] has exponent \(2+\mu\), where \(\omega(\mu)\le 1+2\mu\). Here \(\omega(\frac{1}{2})=2=1+2(\frac{1}{2})\), so it gives _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) running time. Combining the full curve with the deterministic (min,+)-product algorithm and APSP reduction of Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[1, Theorems 22 and 33-34\] further gives _O(n_<sup>2.4999</sup>) running time.<tbc>

4. **Minimum and maximum witnesses.** For two Boolean \(n\times n\) matrices, a minimum (maximum) witness for entry (_i,j_) is the least (greatest) index _k_ with _A<sub>ik</sub>=B<sub>kj</sub>_=1. The standard blocking algorithm \[3, Section 2.1\] takes \(O(n^{1-r+\omega(r)}+n^{2+r})\) time. Taking \(r=\frac{1}{2}\) gives _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time for all witnesses.<tbc>

5. **Sparse matrix multiplication.** For two \(n\times n\) matrices with at most _m_ nonzero entries each, the sparse-dense decomposition of Yuster and Zwick \[14, Section 3\] gives \(O(m^2/n^r+n^{\omega(r)})\) time for \(0\le r\le 1\). Thus \(m\le n^{1.25}\) permits _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time.<tbc>

6. **Dynamic matrix inverse and reachability.** Substituting Theorem 1.1 into van den Brand–Nanongkai–Saranurak’s tradeoff \[11, Theorem 4.2\], with _u_=0.50323551 and _v_=0.80667763 in \(max\{u+v,\omega(1,u,v)-u,\omega(v)-v\}\), gives _O(n_<sup>1.30992</sup>) worst-case time per entry update and query for maintaining the inverse of a nonsingular \(n\times n\) matrix, after _O(n_<sup>2.25</sup>) preprocessing. The associated Monte Carlo reduction gives the same bounds for directed reachability under edge updates, with _O_(1) query time for a fixed pair \[11, Corollary C.12 and Theorem C.16\].

## Appendix A. Splitting two polynomial products

We recap the two-sector construction used in \[9, Lemma 4.1\] as an explicit change of coordinates for pairs of polynomials.<sup>1</sup>

Fix \(r\ge 1\) and \(s\ge 2\). The tensor \(C_{XY}(r,s)\otimes B_X(2)\) computes

\((f,(a,b))\longmapsto(fa,fb),\mathrm{deg}f<r,\mathrm{deg}a,\mathrm{deg}b<s.\)

Thus tensoring with _B<sub>X</sub>_(2) means multiplying two polynomials by the same _f_. We will change coordinates to split the second input into lengths _s_+1 and _s_-1.

For \(e\ge 1\) and \(\mathrm{deg}a,\mathrm{deg}b\le e\), use<tbc>

\(p=a+tb,h=b-p_{e+1}t^e,p_d=[t^d]p.\)

<tbc>Here \[_t<sup>d</sup>_\]_p_ denotes the coefficient of _t<sup>d</sup>_. We have \(\mathrm{deg}p\le e+1\) and \(\mathrm{deg}h\le e-1\), and these coordinates are invertible: _b=h+p_<sub>_e_+1</sub>_t<sup>e</sup>_, _a=p-tb_. Use them on the input pair with _e=s_-1 and on the output pair with _e=r+s_-2. Multiplication by _f_ becomes<tbc>

\((p,h)\longmapsto(fp,fh+p_st^{s-1}(f-f_{r-1}t^{r-1})).\)

<tbc>Scale input _h_ by \(\varepsilon^{-1}\) and its output coordinate by \(\varepsilon\). The map is now

\((p,h)\longmapsto(fp,fh+\varepsilon p_st^{s-1}(f-f_{r-1}t^{r-1}))-\rightarrow^{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}(fp,fh).\)

The independent polynomials _p,h_ have lengths _s_+1_,s_-1, respectively. This gives _C<sub>XY</sub>(r,s_+1) and _C<sub>XY</sub>(r,s_-1) sharing the first leg, with disjoint second and third legs. Permuting the legs gives the other orientations.

## Appendix B. The three-sector splitting

We recap the construction from \[9, Lemma 4.2\]. In _C<sub>XY</sub>(r,_3_s+r_-1), a term has \(0\le x<r\) and output index _z=x+y_. Partition the second-input and output indices into three intervals:

\(\begin{array}{ c c c }
 & \text{left} & \text{middle} & \text{right} \\
Y & [0,s-1] & [s,2s+r-2] & [2s+r-1,3s+r-2] \\
Z & [0,s+r-2] & [s+r-1,2s+r-2] & [2s+r-1,3s+2r-3].
\end{array}\)

Scale middle _Y_ variables by \(\varepsilon\) and middle _Z_ variables by \(\varepsilon^{-1}\), leaving the others unchanged. Since _z=y+x_ with \(0\le x<r\), left and right _Y_ indices stay in the corresponding _Z_ intervals. Cross-sector terms thus connect middle _Y_ to outer _Z_ and acquire a factor \(\varepsilon\); matched terms remain unchanged. As \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\), precisely three matched sectors sharing _X_ remain.

Translations identify the outer sectors with _C<sub>XY</sub>(r,s_). The middle is

\(\sum_{u=0}^{r-1}\sum_{v=0}^{s-1}x_{r-1-u}y_{s+u+v}z_{s+r-1+v},\)

which is _C<sub>XZ</sub>(r,s_) after reversing its first-leg basis. This identifies the individual sector. In the fixed-word construction of (13), the sectors acquire independent first-leg variables before their individual bases are changed.

<sup>1</sup>This is the degree-one case of the classical Clebsch–Gordan formula \[6, Theorem 2.6.3, pp. 56-57 of the author version\]. The coefficient calculation here does not require that formula.

## Appendix E. Replicating a convolution

_Proof of Lemma 2.2._ Put _P(t_)=_t<sup>m</sup>_-1. Repeated polynomial division writes the inputs uniquely as

\(F=\sum_{a=0}^{r-1}F_aP^a,G=\sum_{b=0}^{s-1}G_bP^b,\mathrm{deg}F_a,\mathrm{deg}G_b<m.\)

These are invertible linear coordinates: the basis polynomials _t<sup>d</sup>P<sup>a</sup>_ have distinct leading degrees _ma+d_. On the output retain the analogous blocks _H<sub>c</sub>_ for \(0\le c<r+s-1\). They use _m(r+s_-1) independent coordinates, within the original output length _m(r+s_)-1. Divide each _F<sub>a</sub>G<sub>b</sub>=Q<sub>ab</sub>+PR<sub>ab</sub>_ with deg_Q<sub>ab</sub>,_deg_R<sub>ab</sub>\<m_. Scale input blocks _a,b_ by \(\varepsilon^{-a},\varepsilon^{-b}\) and output block _c_ by \(\varepsilon^c\). The transformed product has

\(H_c=\sum_{a+b=c}Q_{ab}+\varepsilon\sum_{a+b=c-1}R_{ab}.\)

Let \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m\) be the distinct roots of _P_. Since \(Q_{ab}(\alpha_h)=F_a(\alpha_h)G_b(\alpha_h)\), the limit gives

\(H_c(\alpha_h)=\sum_{a+b=c}F_a(\alpha_h)G_b(\alpha_h)(1\le h\le m).\)

Evaluation at _m_ distinct points is invertible on each block of degree less than _m_. The resulting coordinates therefore give _m_ independent convolutions of lengths _r,s_. The evaluation step is the usual diagonalization of cyclic convolution \[5, Theorem 5 and Section 5.1\]; the displayed scalings prove the degeneration, with coefficient degree at most one.

_Proof of Lemma 4.1._ Initially let _r,s\>_0 be rational, and define

\(g_{ij}(r,s)=sup_{q\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}qr,qs\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}\frac{f_{ij}(qr,qs)}{q}.\) (F.1)

Replication gives \(f_{ij}(m,m)\ge m\), and monotonicity therefore gives \(f_{ij}(r,s)\ge min\{r,s\}\) for integer lengths. The bounds and input interchange follow from (15) and the lower bound above. Replacing _q_ by _q/t_ proves homogeneity.

The crucial point is that finitely many supremum values can be approached at one common scale. Choose scales _q<sub>h</sub>_ approximating the desired values, and choose _Q_ so that every _Q/q<sub>h</sub>_ is a positive integer. By (17),
